title.en: Huallallo Caruincho: One Child for the God, One for the Parents
title.zh: 瓦拉約·卡魯因喬:一孩獻神,一孩歸家

region.en: Province of Huarochiri, highlands above Lima (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 利馬高原瓦羅奇里省(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The most ancient tradition of Huarochiri tells of huacas called Yananamca Intanamca who, in an encounter with another huaca called Huallallo Caruincho, were conquered and destroyed; Huallallo remained Lord and God of the land. He ordered that no woman should bring forth more than two children, of which one was to be sacrificed for him to eat, and the other - whichever the parents chose - might be brought up. In those days all who died were brought to life again on the fifth day, and what was sown sprouted, grew and ripened on the fifth day; the three provinces were then a very hot country which the Indians call Yunca or Ande, with a great variety of beautiful birds, macaws and parrots. All this - the people, who led very evil lives, and the idol - came to be driven away to other Andes by the idol Pariacaca.
summary.zh: 瓦羅奇里最古的傳說講述名為「亞南亞姆卡-因坦亞姆卡」的瓦卡,與另一位瓦卡「瓦拉約·卡魯因喬」交戰而被征服毀滅;瓦拉約遂為該地之主神。他立規:婦女不得生多於二子,其一須獻祭給他吃,另一子——由父母自擇——可留養。彼時死者於第五日復活;播種之物第五日發芽、生長、成熟;三省之地氣候炎熱,印第安人稱之為「永卡」(溫熱之地),其間有金剛鸚鵡、鸚鵡等豔麗禽鳥。後來人民(相傳其行甚惡)連同該神,一併被瓦卡「帕里亞卡卡」逐往別處安第斯山林。

sensitivity.note: Huarochiri (Yauyos) tradition - Central Andean, pre-Inca; included in the Inca/Andean corpus as the classic Quechua myth text. Child-sacrifice rule recorded critically.

passages.text: It is a most ancient tradition that, before any other event of which there is any memory, there were certain huacas or idols, which, together with the others, must be supposed to have walked in the form of men. These huacas were called Yananamca Intanamca; and in a certain encounter they had with another huaca called Huallallo Caruincho, they were conquered and destroyed by the said Huallallo, who remained as Lord and God of the land.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 1 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: He ordered that no woman should bring forth more than two children, of which one was to be sacrificed for him to eat, and the other - whichever of the two the parents chose - might be brought up. It was also a tradition that, in those days, all who died were brought to life again on the fifth day, and that what was sown in that land also sprouted, grew, and ripened on the fifth day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 1 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: All these three provinces were then a very hot country, which the Indians call Yunca or Ande; and they say that these crops were made visible in the deserts and uninhabited places, such as that of Pariacaca; and that in these Andes there was a great variety of most beautiful and brilliant birds, such as macaws, parrots, and others. All this, with the people who then inhabited the land (and who, according to their account, led very evil lives), and the said idol, came to be driven away to other Andes by the idol Pariacaca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 1 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Coniraya Viracocha in Rags: Terraces Raised by a Word
title.zh: 衣衫襤褸的庫尼拉亞·維拉科查:一語築田

region.zh: 瓦羅奇里省(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: They say that in most ancient times Coniraya Uiracocha appeared in the form and dress of a very poor Indian clothed in rags, so that those who knew not who he was reviled him and called him a lousy wretch. He was the Creator of all things: by his word of command he caused the terraces and fields to be formed on the steep sides of ravines, and the sustaining walls to rise up and support them; he made the irrigating channels to flow by merely hurling a hollow cane, and went in various directions arranging many things. His great knowledge enabled him to invent tricks and deceits touching the huacas and idols of the villages he visited. He was invoked almost down to the arrival of the Spaniards: when the Indians worshipped him they said 'Coniraya Uiracocha, thou art Lord of all: thine are the crops, and thine are all the people'; in commencing any arduous undertaking they threw a piece of coca on the ground as an oblation, saying 'Tell me, O Lord Coniraya Uiracocha, how I am to do this?' - a custom which prevailed also among the weavers of cloths when their work was toilsome.
summary.zh: 相傳太古之時,庫尼拉亞·維拉科查以極貧印第安人之形現身,衣衫襤褸,不識其真身者皆唾罵他是骯髒的癩子。他卻是造物主:一言既出,溝壑陡坡上的梯田與擋土牆便平地而起;他只須擲出一根空心竹杖,灌溉水渠便自然暢流;他四處行走,安排諸事,還以其大智對所訪村落中的瓦卡與偶像戲弄百出。直至西班牙人到來之前,人們仍在呼求他:崇拜時說「庫尼拉亞·維拉科查,你是萬有之主:五穀屬你,萬民屬你」;凡遇艱難大事,先擲古柯葉於地為祭,說「主啊庫尼拉亞·維拉科查,告訴我當如何行事」;織工織造繁難花紋時亦行此俗。

sensitivity.note: The disheveled culture-hero of Huarochiri; the coca-divination custom is a living practice attested by the parish priest.

passages.text: They say that in most ancient times the Coniraya Uiracocha appeared in the form and dress of a very poor Indian clothed in rags, insomuch that those who knew not who he was reviled him and called him a lousy wretch. They say that this was the Creator of all things; and that, by his word of command, he caused the terraces and fields to be formed on the steep sides of ravines, and the sustaining walls to rise up and support them. He also made the irrigating channels to flow, by merely hurling a hollow cane, such as we call a cane of Spain; and he went in various directions, arranging many things. His great knowledge enabled him to invent tricks and deceits touching the huacas and idols in the villages which he visited.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is certain that it was invoked and reverenced almost down to the time when the Spaniards arrived in this land. For when the Indians worshipped it they said: 'Coniraya Uiracocha, thou art Lord of all: thine are the crops, and thine are all the people.' In commencing any arduous or difficult undertaking, they threw a piece of coca on the ground, as an oblation, and said: 'Tell me, O Lord Coniraya Uiracocha, how I am to do this?' The same custom prevailed among the weavers of cloths, when their work was toilsome and difficult.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, chs. 1-2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Lucma Fruit and the Crawling Child: Cavillaca's Virgin Conception
title.zh: 盧克瑪果與爬行的嬰孩:卡維利亞卡的處女感孕

region.en: Anchicocha, between Chorrillo and Huarochiri (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喬里略與瓦羅奇里之間的安奇科查(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: There was a woman who was a huaca, named Cavillaca, a most beautiful virgin sought after by all the principal idols, but she would never show favour to any. Once she sat down to weave a mantle at the foot of a lucma tree, when the wise Coniraya turned himself into a very beautiful bird, went up into the lucma tree, took some of his generative seed and made it into the likeness of a ripe and luxurious lucma, which he allowed to fall near the beautiful Cavillaca. She took it and ate it with delight, and was made pregnant without other contact with man. When nine months were completed she bore a son, herself remaining a virgin, and suckled the child for a whole year without knowing whose it was. When the child began to crawl, Cavillaca demanded that the huacas and principal idols should assemble, and that it should be declared whose son the child was. Each adorned himself in the richest clothes to appear brighter than the rest, that she might select him for her spouse. In the assembly at Anchicocha, in the lowest place of all, sat Coniraya Uiracocha in his beggar's rags. Cavillaca declared that as none would speak, she would let the child go, and his father would be the one to whom he crawls; she loosed the child, who, passing by all the others, went to Coniraya in his rags and dirt, rejoiced, laughed, and rested at his feet. Cavillaca, in shame - 'What disgrace is this, that a lady such as I am should be made pregnant by a poor and filthy creature' - snatched up the child and fled towards the sea-shore; Coniraya put on magnificent golden robes and pursued her crying loving words, his splendour illuminating the whole country; but the disdainful Cavillaca would not turn her head, calling him a creature so vile and filthy. She came to the sea coast of Pachacamac, entered the sea with her child, and was turned into a rock; the two rocks may still be seen, mother and child.
summary.zh: 當時有一位女性瓦卡,名卡維利亞卡,絕世美人,眾神皆求之,她卻一概不允。一日她在盧克瑪樹下織布,智者的庫尼拉亞化作美鳥飛上樹端,將自己的精液化作一顆熟透肥美的盧克瑪果,落到美人近旁。卡維利亞卡拾而食之,甘美異常,遂未經男女交接而感孕。十月期滿,處女生子,親自哺乳一年,不知其父為誰。孩子會爬之後,她召請諸瓦卡齊聚,宣告:誰是孩子的父親。諸神各梳洗盛裝,欲以最光鮮之姿被選為夫。在安奇科查的集會上,庫尼拉亞以乞丐襤褸之身坐在最末位。卡維利亞卡環視無人應答,便說:「你們既都不肯認,我便放了這孩子——他爬向誰,誰便是他的父親。」孩子爬過諸神,逕奔那襤褸骯髒的庫尼拉亞,嬉笑歡呼,依偎其足。卡維利亞卡羞憤交加:「我這般尊貴之身,竟為此卑賤污穢之物所孕!」抱起孩子轉身奔向海濱。庫尼拉亞忽换上燦然金袍,追她呼喚愛語,光輝照徹山野;美人卻頭也不回,罵他是穢物。她逃至帕查卡馬克海濱,抱子入海,化為礁石。至今海邊猶見兩石:母與子。

sensitivity.note: The Cavillaca cycle is the Huarochiri masterpiece; the conception scene is retold soberly as the source has it.

passages.text: At that time they also say that there was a woman who was a huaca. Her name was Cavillaca, and she was a most beautiful virgin, who was much sought after by the huacas, or principal idols, but she would never show favour to any of them. Once she sat down to weave a mantle at the foot of a lucma tree, when the wise Coniraya succeeded in approaching her in the following manner: he turned himself into a very beautiful bird, and went up into the lucma tree, where he took some of his generative seed and made it into the likeness of a ripe and luxurious lucma, which he allowed to fall near the beautiful Cavillaca. She took it and ate it with much delight, and by it she was made pregnant without other contact with man.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the nine months were completed she conceived and bore a son, herself remaining a virgin; and she suckled the child at her own breast for a whole year without knowing whose it was. At the end of the year, when the child began to crawl, Cavillaca demanded that the huacas and principal idols of the land should assemble, and that it should be declared whose son was the child. Each one adorned himself in the best manner possible, combing, washing, and dressing in the richest clothes, each desiring to appear brighter and better than the rest in the eyes of the beautiful Cavillaca, that so she might select him for her spouse and husband.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that, in this assembly, in the lowest place of all, sat the god Coniraya Uiracocha in his beggar's rags. When she found that all were silent, she said: 'As none of you will speak, I shall let the child go, and doubtless his father will be the one to whom he crawls.' So saying, she loosed the child, who, passing by all the others, went to where was his father Coniraya in his rags and dirt, and when the child reached him, it rejoiced and laughed, and rested at his feet. This conduct caused Cavillaca great shame and annoyance, and she snatched up the child, exclaiming: 'What disgrace is this that has come upon me, that a lady such as I am should be made pregnant by a poor and filthy creature.' Then she turned her back and fled away towards the sea-shore.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coniraya Uiracocha desired the friendship and favour of the goddess, so, when he saw her take her flight, he put on magnificent golden robes, and, leaving the astonished assembly of gods, he ran after her, crying out: 'O my lady Cavillaca, turn your eyes and see how handsome and gallant am I'; and they say that his splendour illuminated the whole country. Yet the disdainful Cavillaca would not turn her head, but rather increased her speed, saying she had been made pregnant by a creature so vile and filthy. She came to the sea coast of Pachacamac, where she entered the sea with her child, and was turned into a rock. They say that the two rocks may still be seen, which are mother and child.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Condor Blessed, the Fox Cursed: Coniraya's Animal Decrees
title.zh: 禿鷹受福、狐狸遭咒:庫尼拉亞的禽獸判詞

region.en: Coast road from Huarochiri to the sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦羅奇里下海之路(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: As Coniraya ran along the shore crying 'Stop! stop! lady. Turn round and look!', he met a condor and asked whether he had seen a woman with such marks. 'I saw her very near this place,' said the condor; and Coniraya blessed him: he should live for ever, traverse wildernesses and valleys, build where he should never be disturbed, eat all things found dead - huanacu, llamas, lambs - and have power to kill the neglected; 'he who kills you shall himself be killed.' He met a small fox that told him the goddess was far off and he could not overtake her; Coniraya cursed the fox: never to go abroad but at night, always to smell bad, and to be persecuted and hated by men. A lion gave good news and was blessed: to be respected and feared by all, executioner of evil doers, eating the llamas of sinners; after death, his skin should be preserved with head, teeth and eyes as if alive, and he who adorned himself with it must kill a llama, then dance and sing with the skin on his back at the principal festivals. A second fox was cursed; a falcon that gave good news was decreed to breakfast on the delicate alquenti, and its killer to sacrifice a llama and wear the falcon's skin on his head in festival; parrots that gave bad news were condemned to shrieks that betray them, hated by all. Thus he rewarded all animals whose news accorded with his wishes, and cursed the rest. The customs live: condors sacred and never killed, lion skins brought out on great occasions, whole villages running after a fox-cry, falcon headdresses at every festival.
summary.zh: 庫尼拉亞沿岸追呼:「停!停!美人,回頭看看我!」途中遇一禿鷹,問其曾否見到那女子。禿鷹答:「就在附近,快走幾步必能追上。」庫尼拉亞大喜,祝福禿鷹:得享永生,縱橫荒漠溝壑,築巢無人敢擾,凡遇死屍——駝馬、綿羊——皆可啄食,並有權撲殺遭主人疏於看管的牲畜;「殺你者必自死。」又遇小狐,說美人已遠,追之不及;庫尼拉亞咒之:永夜行,身常惡臭,人人追捕憎恨。獅子報以佳音,受福:受萬獸敬畏,為懲惡之刑官,可食罪人之駝馬;死後其皮連頭帶齒,目嵌眶中,儼然如生;披其皮者須宰駝馬為祭,負皮載歌載舞於大節。第二隻狐狸遭咒;隼報佳音,受封晨食細嫩之蜂鳥,獵隼者亦須宰駝馬,節日以隼皮覆首起舞;鸚鵡報惡信,被咒終日嘶鳴自洩行蹤,為眾人所惡。凡報喜訊者皆蒙恩,報惡信者皆受咒。至今俗尚猶存:禿鷹為聖,殺之者死;獅皮出於大節;聞狐聲則全村追捕;節節起舞必有隼冠。

sensitivity.note: Etiological decrees of the trickster god; tagged with taboo-transgression for the condor-killing taboo.

passages.text: Coniraya continued the pursuit, crying out, and saying, 'Stop! stop! lady. Turn round and look! where are you, that I cannot see you?' As he ran, he met a condor, to whom he said: 'Brother, tell me whether you encountered a woman with such and such marks?' The condor answered: 'I saw her very near this place, and if you go a little faster, you will certainly overtake her.' To whom Coniraya, rejoicing at the good news, thus made reply, blessing the condor, and saying: 'You shall live for ever, and I give you power to go whithersoever you please, to traverse the wildernesses and valleys, to search the ravines, to build where you shall never be disturbed... I further declare that he who kills you shall himself be killed.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coniraya then continued his journey, and met a small fox of the kind that emits a strong odour, and asked him the same question touching Cavillaca. The fox answered that it was in vain for him to run fast, because the goddess was now far off. Then Coniraya cursed the fox, saying: 'As a punishment for the bad news you have given me, I command that you shall never go abroad but at night, that a bad smell shall always come from you, and that men shall persecute and hate you.' ... A lion which, in reply to his question, told him that he was very near the goddess, was blessed: 'You shall be respected and feared by all, and I assign to you the office of punisher and executioner of evil doers... after your death you shall still be honoured; for when they kill you and take your skin they shall do so without cutting off the head... those who kill you shall wear your head over their own, and your skin shall cover them... he who would adorn himself with your skin, must kill a llama on the occasion, and then dance and sing with you on his back.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next he met some parrots that gave him bad news; so he declared that they should always give out cries and shrieks, that when they wished to feed they should not be safe, for their own cries should betray them, and that they should be hated by all people. Thus he rewarded and granted privileges to all the animals that gave him news that accorded with his wishes, and cursed all those whose tidings were not agreeable to him. These traditions are so rooted in the hearts of the people that they hold the condors to be sacred, and never kill one, believing that he who kills one will die himself; they have a great horror of the small fox; and they do to the lion all that was ordained in the blessing of Coniraya, bringing out the skin on great occasions. As to the falcon, there is scarcely a festival in which one does not appear on the heads of the dancers and singers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Urpi-huachac, Mother of the Doves and of All the Fishes in the Sea
title.zh: 烏爾皮-瓜查克:鴿母與海魚之母

region.zh: 帕查卡馬克海岸(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When Coniraya reached the sea-shore he found that Cavillaca and her child were turned into stone; and walking along the beach he met two beautiful young daughters of Pachacamac, who guarded a great serpent because their mother was absent, visiting the newly arrived Cavillaca in the sea. The name of this wife of Pachacamac was Urxayhuachac. Coniraya, who could keep the serpent quiet by his wisdom, had intercourse with the elder sister, and desired to do the same with the younger, but she flew away in the shape of a wild pigeon (urpi): hence the mother of these girls was called Urpi-huachac, or mother of the doves. In those days there were no fishes in the sea, but Urpi-huachac reared a few in a small pond. Coniraya was enraged that she should be absent in the sea visiting Cavillaca, so he emptied the fishes out of her pond into the sea, and thence all the fishes now in the sea have been propagated. When the mother returned and was told what had happened, she pursued Coniraya in great fury, until he stopped to wait for her. She addressed him with loving words - 'Coniraya, do you wish that I should comb your head and pick out the lice?' He consented and reclined his head on her lap; but while she pretended to comb him she was forming a rock over which she might hurl him when off his guard. He knew this through his great wisdom, told her he must retire for a few minutes, and went back to the land of Huarochiri, where he wandered a long time playing tricks on whole villages and single men and women.
summary.zh: 庫尼拉亞到達海濱,見卡維利亞卡母子已化石;沿岸而行,遇帕查卡馬克的兩位美貌女兒,看守著一條巨蛇——她們的母親外出海上探望新到的卡維利亞卡。帕查卡馬克之妻名烏爾夏伊瓜查克。庫尼拉亞以智慧制住巨蛇,與長女交合,又欲對幼女如法炮製;幼女化作野鴿(烏爾皮)飛去。故此二女之母被稱為「烏爾皮-瓜查克」——鴿之母。其時海中無魚,唯烏爾皮-瓜查克在小池中養了幾尾。庫尼拉亞恨她棄家探望卡維利亞卡,便把池中魚盡數傾入大海——今日海中所有魚類皆由此繁衍而來。母親歸來聽說此事,大怒追趕庫尼拉亞;他停下等候。她以溫言相誘:「庫尼拉亞,可要我為你梳頭捉蝨?」他依言枕於其膝;她假意梳理,實則暗中在旁築起一塊岩石,欲趁他不備將他擲下。庫尼拉亞以大智識破,託言稍退片刻,逃回瓦羅奇里山中,長久漫遊,對全村或單人男女惡作劇不休。

sensitivity.note: Origin of the sea's fishes; the coastal goddess Urpi-huachac links Huarochiri to the Pachacamac pantheon.

passages.text: When he reached the sea-shore he found that Cavillaca and her child were turned into stone; and as he walked along the beach he met two beautiful young daughters of Pachacamac, who guarded a great serpent, because their mother was absent, visiting the recently arrived Cavillaca in the sea. The name of this wife of Pachacamac was Urxayhuachac. When Coniraya found these girls alone without their mother, he did not care for the serpent, which he could keep quiet by his wisdom; so he had intercourse with the elder sister, and desired to do the same with the younger, but she flew away in the shape of a wild pigeon (called by the Indians urpi); hence the mother of these girls was called Urpi-huachac, or mother of the doves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: In those days it is said that there were no fishes in the sea, but that this Urpi-huachac reared a few in a small pond. Coniraya was enraged that Urpi-huachac should be absent in the sea, visiting Cavillaca; so he emptied the fishes out of her pond into the sea, and thence all the fishes now in the sea have been propagated.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the mother of the girls returned they told her what had happened, and she pursued Coniraya in a great fury, calling out, until at last he determined to stop and wait for her. Then she addressed him with loving and tender words, saying: 'Coniraya, do you wish that I should comb your head and pick out the lice?' So he consented, and reclined his head on her lap; but while she was pretending to do this, she was forming a rock over which she might hurl him when he was off his guard. He knew this through his great wisdom, and told her he must retire for a few minutes. She agreed to this; and he went back to the land of Huarochiri, where he wandered about for a long time, playing tricks both to whole villages and to single men or women.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 2 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Five Days of Darkness: Stones Knocking Against Each Other
title.zh: 五日長夜:石擊石的世界

region.en: Provinces of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦羅奇里、瑪瑪與查克利亞三省(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: They relate that, a long time ago, the sun disappeared and the world was dark for a space of five days; that the stones knocked one against the other; and that the mortars, which they call mutca, and the pestles called marop, rose against their masters, who were also attacked by their sheep, both those fastened in the houses and those in the fields. Avila, who records it, wonders whether this may have been the eclipse which occurred when the Redeemer died, and objects that, as these people had no watches, they could not have counted five days by the absence of the sun.
summary.zh: 相傳很久以前,太陽隱去,世界陷入五日黑暗;石頭相互碰撞;搗穀的石臼(穆特卡)與石杵(馬羅普)起而反抗主人;主人們又遭自家羊群攻擊——無論圈在屋內的,還是放牧在外的。記錄此故事的阿維拉猜測這或許是救主受難時的日蝕,又質疑:既無時計,他們何以知道太陽缺席了五日。

sensitivity.note: Cosmic-disturbance tale; the animated tools and attacking flocks parallel the day-of-darkness cluster in other traditions.

passages.text: They relate that, a long time ago, the sun disappeared and the world was dark for a space of five days; that the stones knocked one against the other; and that the mortars, which they call mutca, and the pestles called marop, rose against their masters, who were also attacked by their sheep, both those fastened in the houses and those in the fields.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 3 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: This may have been the eclipse which occurred when our Redeemer died; but I cannot clearly make this out, for when it was day in that hemisphere it was night here... The rest of the story consists of lies, for, as these people had no watches, how could they tell that the sun was absent for five days, seeing that we count days by the absence and presence of the sun?
passages.note: Avila's commentary condensed (Markham 1873); the gloss is the recorder's, the tale is the tradition.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Speaking Llama and the Mountain of Villca-coto
title.zh: 開口的駝馬與維爾卡-科托山

region.en: Villca-coto, between San Damian and San Geronimo de Surco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 聖達米安與聖哲羅姆-德-蘇爾科之間的維爾卡-科托山(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: An Indian was tethering his llama in a place where there was good pasture, and the animal resisted, showing sorrow and moaning after its manner, crying 'yu' yu''. The master, who happened to be eating a choclo (ear of maize), observing this, threw the core (coronta) at the llama, saying: 'Fool, why do you moan and refrain from eating? Have I not put you where there is good pasture?' The llama thus replied: 'Madman! what do you know? Learn that I am not sad without good cause; for within five days the sea will rise and cover the whole earth, destroying all there is upon it.' The man, wondering that his llama should speak, asked whether there was any way by which they could save themselves. The llama said that the man must follow it quickly to the summit of a high mountain called Villca-coto, between the parish of San Damian and San Geronimo de Surco, taking food for five days. He did as he was told, carrying his load on his back and leading the llama, and found on the summit many different kinds of birds and animals assembled. Just as they reached the top the sea began to rise: the water filled the valleys and covered the tops of the hills, except that of Villca-coto; the animals were crowded together, for the water rose so high that some could hardly find foothold. Among these was a fox, whose tail was washed by the waves - which is the reason that the tips of foxes' tails are black. At the end of five days the waters began to abate, and the sea returned to its former bounds; but the whole earth was without inhabitants except that solitary man, from whom descend all the people who now exist.
summary.zh: 一人正在好牧場拴駱馬,駝馬不肯安臥,悲鳴「喲!喲!」。主人正吃著玉米棒,見狀擲出玉米芯,罵道:「蠢畜,好草不吃,鳴什麼?」駝馬答道:「蠢人!你懂什麼?我悲鳴自有緣故:不出五日,海水將漲,淹沒大地,毀滅其上一切。」那人驚詫駝馬竟能人言,忙問可有生路。駝馬命他快隨己登一座極高的名為維爾卡-科托之山——在聖達米安與聖哲羅姆-德-蘇爾科教區之間——並帶足五日糧食。他依言背糧牽駝登頂,見山巔早已聚滿各色飛禽走獸。他們剛到頂,海水便開始上漲:填滿山谷,漫過群山峰頂,唯維爾卡-科托山不沒。獸群擠作一團,水高得連立足之處都快沒了。其中一隻狐狸,尾巴被浪打濕——所以狐尾尖至今是黑的。五日之後,水勢漸退,大海復歸故道;大地之上唯存此孤身一人,今日世上的人類皆其後裔。

sensitivity.note: The Huarochiri flood: an animal-warning deluge narrative of the messenger-fails type in reverse (the animal warns, the man heeds); a flagship cross-cluster record.

passages.text: An Indian was tethering his llama in a place where there was good pasture, and the animal resisted, showing sorrow and moaning after its manner, which it does by crying 'yu' yu''. The master, who happened to be eating a choclo, observing this, threw the core (which they call coronta) at the llama, saying: 'Fool, why do you moan and refrain from eating? Have I not put you where there is good pasture?' The llama thus replied: 'Madman! what do you know, and what can you suppose? Learn that I am not sad without good cause; for within five days the sea will rise and cover the whole earth, destroying all there is upon it.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 4 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The man, wondering that his llama should speak, answered it by asking whether there was any way by which they could save themselves. The llama then said that the man must follow it quickly to the summit of a high mountain called Villca-coto, taking with him food for five days, and that he might thus be saved. The man did as he was told, carrying his load on his back and leading the llama, and he arrived on the summit of the mountain, where he found many different kinds of birds and animals assembled.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 4 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Just as he and his llama reached the top the sea began to rise, and the water filled the valleys and covered the tops of the hills, except that of Villca-coto; but the animals were crowded together, for the water rose so high that some of them could hardly find foothold. Among these was a fox, whose tail was washed by the waves, which they say is the reason that the tips of foxes' tails are black. At the end of five days the waters began to abate, and the sea returned to its former bounds; but the whole earth was without inhabitants except that solitary man, from whom, they say, descend all the people who now exist.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 4 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Five Eggs on Condorcoto: The Birth of Pariacaca and His Brothers
title.zh: 孔多爾科托的五枚蛋:帕里亞卡卡誕生

region.en: Condorcoto mountain, between Huarochiri and Chorrillo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦羅奇里與喬里略之間的孔多爾科托山(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: After the deluge, in every district the Indians chose the richest and most valiant man among them for their leader, and this period they call Purun-pacha - the time when there was no king. In those days there appeared five large eggs on a mountain between Huarochiri and Chorrillo towards the south, called Condorcoto - the origin of Pariacaca. At that time there lived a poor and ill-clad Indian named Huathiacuri, who was a son of Pariacaca, and who learnt many arts from his father; he was called Huathiacuri because his food was all huatyasca, parboiled, not properly cooked food, being poor he could afford nothing better.
summary.zh: 洪水之後,各地印第安人推舉其中最富最勇者為首領,此期稱為「普龍-帕查」——無王之世。其時,在瓦羅奇里與喬里略之間偏南的一座名為孔多爾科托的山上,出現了五枚巨卵——此即帕里亞卡卡之來歷。當時有一個衣衫襤褸的貧苦印第安人,名叫瓜提亞庫里,乃帕里亞卡卡之子,從其父學得諸多法術;因其所食皆為半生不熟的「瓜蒂亞斯卡」(貧者唯能如此),遂得此名。

sensitivity.note: Egg-born mountain god; tagged miraculous-birth against the cluster of divine births.

passages.text: It must now be understood that in the time after the deluge, in every district, the Indians chose the richest and most valiant man among them for their leader, and this period they call Purun-pacha, which means the time when there was no king. They say that in those days there appeared five large eggs on a mountain between Huarochiri and Chorrillo, towards the south, (and this is the origin of Pariacaca) called Condorcoto.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: At that time there lived a poor and ill-clad Indian named Huathiacuri, who, they say, was a son of Pariacaca, and who learnt many arts from his father. They say that he was called Huathiacuri because his food was all huatyasca, which means parboiled, not properly cooked, or, as we say here, roasted en barbacoa. Being poor, he could afford nothing better.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Foxes' Conversation: The Cure of the Rich Man Who Called Himself Creator
title.zh: 狐語診病:自稱造物主的富人得醫

region.zh: 安奇科查與拉塔利亞科高地(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: A very rich and great lord had his house on Anchicocha, its roof made of the yellow and red feathers of certain birds, the walls covered with curious materials; he had llamas of red, blue, yellow and other bright colours, so that to make mantles it was unnecessary to dye the wool. People came to him from all directions, and he made himself out to be very wise, even saying that he was the God and Creator. But he fell sick of a tedious and disgusting disease, and everybody wondered that a man who was a God and Creator should be so ill and unable to cure himself; they began to murmur against him. Huathiacuri, journeying towards the sea, slept on the height called Latallaco, where he saw a fox going towards the sea and another coming from the coast: one asked the other for news. 'All is well except that the rich man is very sick... the real cause is that, when his wife was toasting a little maize, one grain fell on her skirt. She gave it to a man who ate it, and afterwards she committed adultery with him. This is the reason that the rich man is sick, and a serpent is now hovering over his beautiful house to eat it, while a toad with two heads is waiting under his grinding-stone with the same object. But no one knows this.' Huathiacuri, having heard what the foxes said, went to the place where the rich man lay sick, and asked the beautiful young daughter - in payment for her favour - to let him cure her father. He commenced the cure by saying: 'Do you know that your wife has committed adultery, and that this is the reason of your sickness? Do you know that there are two great serpents above your house waiting to eat you? and that there is a toad with two heads underneath that grind-stone? Before everything else we must kill those animals, and then you will begin to recover. But when you are well you must worship and reverence my father, who will appear before many days; for it is quite clear that you are neither God nor Creator. If you were God you would not be ill, nor would you be in need of a cure.' Search was made and the two serpents found on the top of the house and killed; the wife confessed her adultery; the grindstone was raised and out hopped a toad with two heads, which went to a spring that now flows by Anchicocha, where they say it still lives, making those who go to it lose their way, and become mad, and die. The sick man became well, and gave Huathiacuri his young daughter to wife.
summary.zh: 安奇科查住著一位巨富之主:屋頂覆黃紅羽毛,牆壁飾奇珍;駝馬有紅、藍、黃諸色,織毯無須染色。四方之人皆來拜謁,他自詡明智,甚至自稱是神、是造物主。然而他得了纏綿惡疾,舉族驚異:神與造物主豈會臥病而無自救之能?人們開始抱怨他。瓜提亞庫里赴海途中宿於拉塔利亞科高地,見一狐向海而去,一狐自海岸來;來者問訊,去者答:「一切安好,唯那富人病重……真正緣故是:其妻烘玉米時,一粒玉米落在裙上,她拾起給一男子吃了,隨後與他私通。富人之病由此而起;如今有一條大蛇盤踞其美宅之上欲食之,磨石之下又伏著一隻雙頭蟾蜍,同樣等著吃他。只是無人知曉。」瓜提亞庫里聽罷,便至病榻,對病主的幼女說:若肯以身相許,他便醫好其父。醫治之始,他直言:「你可知道,你妻子與人私通,這正是你生病的原因?你可知道,屋頂之上有兩條巨蛇等著吃你,磨石之下伏著雙頭蟾蜍?先殺了這些動物,你的病才會好。病癒之後,你須敬奉我父親——他不久將顯現。你顯然既非神、亦非造物主;你若是神,豈會生病、需要醫治?」眾人驚訝。其妻怒斥誣謗,但富人求治心切,命人搜查:屋頂果然有兩蛇,殺之;其妻承認私通;掀起磨石,雙頭蟾蜍蹦出,逃至今安奇科查旁的一眼泉邊——相傳它至今仍住在那裡,使誤飲其水者迷路、發狂、死去。富人病癒,以幼女妻之。

sensitivity.note: The fox-lore diagnosis of adultery-sickness; the rich man who claimed creatorhood is unmasked - a theodicy episode of the Huarochiri cycle.

passages.text: A very rich and great lord had his house on Anchicocha, about a league and a half from the place where the five eggs appeared. His house was very richly and curiously adorned, for the roof was made of the yellow and red feathers of certain birds, and the walls were covered with similar and even more curious materials. This lord had a great number of llamas - some red, others blue and yellow and of other bright colours, so that, to make mantles, it was unnecessary to dye the wool. For these reasons people came to him from all directions to pay their respects; and he made himself to be very wise, even saying that he was the God and Creator. But at last a great misfortune befell him: he fell sick of a tedious and disgusting disease, and everybody wondered that a man who was so wise and rich, and was a God and Creator, should be so ill and be unable to cure himself. So they began to murmur against him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this time they say that Huathiacuri journeyed towards the sea, and slept on that height called Latallaco. While he was there he saw a fox going towards the sea, and another coming from the coast towards Anchicocha. The one coming from the sea asked the other whether there was any news, and the other answered that all was well except that the rich man was very sick... But, added the fox, the real cause is that, when his wife was toasting a little maize, one grain fell on her skirt. She gave it to a man who ate it, and afterwards she committed adultery with him. This is the reason that the rich man is sick, and a serpent is now hovering over his beautiful house to eat it, while a toad with two heads is waiting under his grinding-stone with the same object. But no one knows this.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having heard what the foxes said, he went to the place where the rich man was lying sick, and asked a young and beautiful girl - daughter to the sick God - if any one was ill... He entered, and said that he could certainly effect a cure if the sick man would give his young daughter to him for a wife. The wise Huathiacuri commenced the cure by saying: 'Do you know that your wife has committed adultery, and that this is the reason of your sickness? Do you know that there are two great serpents above your house waiting to eat you? and that there is a toad with two heads underneath that grind-stone? Before everything else we must kill those animals, and then you will begin to recover your health. But, when you are well, you must worship and reverence my father, who will appear before many days, for it is quite clear that you are neither God nor Creator. If you were God you would not be ill, nor would you be in need of a cure.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sick man was so desirous to be cured that he ordered search to be made, and they found the two serpents on the top of the house and killed them. Then the sage reminded the wife that when she was toasting maize one grain had fallen on her skirt... So she confessed. The sage then caused the grindstone to be raised, and there hopped from underneath a toad with two heads, which went to a spring that now flows by Anchicocha, where they say that it still lives, making those who go to it lose their way, and become mad, and die. Having done all this, the sick man became well, and the wise Huathiacuri enjoyed the girl.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)
